summary:
We developed the **Lunar South Pole // Illumination & Comms Planner**, an interactive, browser-based visualization tool that simplifies mission planning for the Moon’s south pole. Existing tools for modeling solar illumination and Earth visibility often rely on complex, specialist interfaces that slow down comparative analysis. Our application addresses this challenge by synchronizing a 3D WebGL terrain and celestial dome view with a 360° panoramic horizon mask plot and a 30-day mission timeline scrubber.

Users can evaluate and compare five candidate Artemis landing regions—including Shackleton Connecting Ridge, Malapert Massif, and de Gerlache Rim 2—pin sites side-by-side, and jump directly to critical mission windows such as sunrise, Earth rise, and simultaneous solar power and Direct-to-Earth (DTE) communication intervals. This is vital because extreme south polar topography creates long shadows and narrow communication line-of-sight windows. By pairing rapid trade-space analysis with an interactive "Explain Physics" Educator Mode, our tool empowers mission planners, students, and the public to explore lunar surface operations effortlessly.
details:
1. Project Details

Overview: What It Does & How It Works The Lunar South Pole // Illumination & Comms Planner is an interactive, browser-based mission planning and educational visualization tool designed to evaluate extreme solar lighting and Direct-to-Earth (DTE) communication constraints at the Moon’s south pole. Instead of requiring users to navigate complex, specialist orbital mechanics software, our application synchronizes three visual perspectives in real time:

  • 3D WebGL Topography & Celestial Dome: Renders directional solar shadows across candidate landing ridges and adjacent Permanently Shadowed Regions (PSRs), alongside the Sun, librating Earth, cardinal compass markers, and Lander POV, Horizon Pan, and Orbital Overview camera presets.
  • 360° Panoramic Horizon Mask Plot: Plots the full 29.53-day synodic Sun trajectory (amber) and Earth optical libration loop (cyan) directly against each site's local terrain obstruction profile.
  • Interactive Synodic Scrubber & 30-Day Gantt Timeline: Allows users to scrub across multi-month epochs (October 2026 – March 2027), animate at 1x, 10x, and 50x speeds, or jump directly to the next Sunrise, Earth Rise, or Simultaneous Sun + DTE Optimal Window.

Benefits & Intended Impact By uniting spatial 3D terrain context with quantitative horizon sky-tracks and multi-site trade-space matrices, the tool bridges the gap between engineering analysis and public outreach:

  • For Mission Planners & Engineers: Accelerates preliminary landing site trade studies by allowing side-by-side horizon pinning (overlaying a secondary site's obstruction profile in purple) and instant comparisons across five candidate Artemis regions (Shackleton Connecting Ridge, de Gerlache Rim 2, Malapert Massif, Haworth Rim, and Nobile Rim 1).
  • For Educators & the Public: Includes an Educator Mode ("Explain Physics") with toggleable callouts that demystify complex lunar phenomena—such as the Moon's 1.54° axial tilt, Earth's optical libration wobble, and why crater floors become cryogenic PSR cold traps—making space exploration accessible to students and enthusiasts.

Tools, Coding Languages & Software Used

  • Frontend & Visualization: HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript (ES6+), Three.js (WebGL) for real-time 3D terrain rendering and dynamic shadow mapping, and HTML5 Canvas for the 360° panoramic horizon plot and 30-day mission timeline.
  • Architecture: Built as a lightweight, zero-install, self-contained single-page web application so it runs smoothly in any modern browser without backend dependencies.
  • AI-Assisted Development: Large Language Models (Gemini) were used to assist with code generation, UI layout structuring, and astronomical physics explainer text.

Creativity & Key Design Factors Considered

  • Dual-Perspective Synchronization: Many tools show either a 3D map or a 2D elevation chart; linking them simultaneously lets users immediately understand why a distant crater rim blocks sunlight or Earth line-of-sight at a specific azimuth.
  • Mission-Critical Edge Cases: At the lunar south pole, the Sun skims the horizon at near-zero elevations and Earth oscillates within a narrow window. We prioritized high-contrast visual indicators for Simultaneous Power + Comms Windows—the critical overlap needed for surface operations.
  • Zero-Friction Accessibility: Designed with intuitive "jump-to-event" controls and plain-language physics tooltips so a first-time user can derive meaningful mission insights within seconds.
